headline: Bunker Push Bass Onto Southwest Ledge in Broad Daylight
subhead: Building current toward the August 28 full moon is stacking bait against the Ledge and the North Rip — bluefish are the sure thing, bass and bonito are the maybe.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out past the breakwater Tuesday morning, flat calm, and the water off the Southwest Ledge had that green, oxygenated look it gets when the current's really moving — not the flat pewter shine of dead water, but that slight roll and shimmer that tells you bait is getting pushed. Ten minutes later the birds told the rest of the story. Terns working low and tight over a patch of nervous water, and under them, peanut bunker getting bulldozed by fish that clearly didn't care it was ten in the morning.

That's the thing about this run of bass we're in — they're not waiting for first light anymore. The bunker schools stacking up from Narragansett down through the Sound are thick enough that the stripers are blowing up on top in broad daylight, which tells you the bait density is winning out over their usual low-light caution. We're seeing pieces of that same pattern out here. Southwest Ledge in 25 to 40 feet has been holding fish that push up under bait pods on the last two hours of the incoming, and the North Rip did the same thing Wednesday evening — a hard boil that lasted maybe fifteen minutes before it went quiet again. I got one over 30 pounds out of that window on a white 2-ounce Deadly Dick fished bare, no teaser, just a straight retrieve through the wash. My mate missed two more on a chartreuse umbrella rig trolled slow along the edge where the ledge drops from 30 into 55.

I want to be straight about this bite because it's not a constant — it's a window bite. You catch the tide right, catch the bait pushed up against structure, and it can be twenty minutes of pure chaos. Miss it, and you're marking bait on the machine with nothing touching it. The building current into the August 28 full moon is the reason these windows are getting sharper. We flagged this a couple weeks back — said once tidal flow built after the new moon, Block Island Sound would turn on quickly once bait got pushed hard against structure, and that's exactly the mechanism driving these daylight blitzes now. Current does the work here more than anywhere else on this coast.

Bluefish have been the more dependable half of the equation, and honestly the more fun half some days. Adult class blues, 4 to 7 pounds, are mixing right into those same bunker schools around the wind farm structure and along the Ledge, and they'll hit anything that moves fast — Ava jigs, small pencil poppers, cut bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig if you want to sit still and let them come to you. We called the adult push building back on the 14th when snapper blues were still thick in the back bays and estuaries — well, here they are, grown into 4-pounders and running with the striper blitzes exactly like we thought they would. Great Salt Pond and Old Harbor are both loaded with snappers still, so the next wave behind these adults is already staged.

Fluke have been the disappointment of the week, if I'm being honest. Warm water on the sand between the Ledge and the island has made them lazy — you can mark fish on structure and still get nothing but soft, half-hearted bites. I fished four spots Thursday drifting 5-inch white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails and only boxed two keepers over 19 inches, both right on the edge of a rock pile where the current concentrates bait. If you're going after fluke this week, fish oversized baits tight to structure and be patient — this isn't the drift-and-cover-water pattern that works when they're aggressive. It's a finesse game right now.

Porgies are steady on the reefs southeast of the harbor, 20 to 35 feet, sandworms and green crab on a hi-lo rig, nothing dramatic but reliable if you want dinner. No real blackfish talk yet — too early, that'll build through September as water starts to ease.

The question everyone's asking me at the dock is bonito. We haven't seen them show at Block Island yet, but Nantucket Sound and the Cape Cod side are with them already, and there was a sailfish sighting off Chatham that tells you just how far this warm pattern has pushed things north. If that warm pocket holds and slides west the way these things sometimes do, I'd expect the first bonito sightings inside the Sound within the next week or two — probably around the can off Old Harbor or out past the breakwater where the water clears up fast. Worth keeping a small Deadly Dick or an epoxy jig rigged and ready even while you're bass fishing.

Offshore, there's bluefin building both to our west and out in the eastern canyons, and the honest answer is we haven't seen that push extend onto our own canyon-adjacent water yet. That's the single biggest variable I'm watching this week — if that warm edge shifts east even a little, Block Canyon could turn on fast. For now, my money stays inshore.

Looking ahead: if this current keeps building toward the full moon, I'd expect the bass blitzes at the Ledge and the North Rip to sharpen rather than fade — shorter windows, harder feeds. I'd fish the last two hours of the incoming at the Ledge and be ready to move fast if the birds tell you to. Bluefish should stay steady through the week regardless of tide. Fluke, keep your expectations modest and fish slow. And if you're out there and see fish busting bait on top with fins that don't look like stripers or blues — get a picture. I want to know before anybody else does.
